questions.q: What question does staging answer that the testing tier does not, per this lesson?
options: Whether a single Flow's logic produces the correct outcome
Whether deploying exactly this release, in exactly this way, right now, would actually go smoothly end to end
Whether a user has the correct profile assigned
Whether a developer's Apex code compiles without syntax errors
questions.explain: Testing checks whether a change works correctly; staging checks whether the full release -- deployment process, data scale, and all bundled changes together -- would actually go smoothly if deployed now.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a Full sandbox is the standard fit for staging rather than a Partial Copy sandbox?
options: Because Full sandboxes are cheaper to maintain than Partial Copy sandboxes
Because Partial Copy sandboxes cannot run Apex batch jobs at all
Because a sampled data subset can hide problems that only appear at full production data volume, which staging exists specifically to catch before production
Because Full sandboxes refresh faster than Partial Copy sandboxes
questions.explain: A batch job or report that behaves fine against a sample can behave very differently against production's real, full-scale data -- exactly the surprise staging is meant to eliminate before it reaches production.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe seasonal release testing as a recurring responsibility rather than a one-time setup task?
options: Because Salesforce only ships one platform release every five years
Because staging environments expire automatically after one release cycle
Because seasonal releases only affect orgs that purchase a special add-on

Because each of Salesforce's three major yearly releases can change platform behavior under an org's customizations, so what passed cleanly against the last release isn't guaranteed to pass against the next one
questions.explain: Every seasonal release deserves its own staging pass specifically because the platform itself changes underneath an org's customizations each time, independent of anything the team changed.

questions.q: What does "sign-off" at the staging tier typically involve, per this lesson?
options: A specific person or group, often a business stakeholder, explicitly confirming the release is approved to go to production -- combining technical validation with business judgment
A developer merging their own branch into the main codebase
An automated test suite passing with zero manual involvement
Deleting the staging sandbox once testing completes
questions.explain: Sign-off confirms both that the release works technically and that shipping it now is the right business call, which is why it's often a business stakeholder's decision, not purely a technical check.

questions.q: A commission-calculation batch job passes in a Partial Copy testing sandbox against a 10,000-record sample, but fails to finish within governor limits against a Full sandbox's real 4-million-record table in staging. What should happen next, per this lesson's promotion-path principle?
options: The fix should be applied directly inside the staging sandbox so the release isn't delayed
The release should proceed to production anyway, since it already passed one round of testing
It goes back to Development for a fix, since a stage shouldn't advance a change it hasn't actually passed
The staging sandbox should be refreshed repeatedly until the job happens to finish in time
questions.explain: Consistent with the promotion path's core rule from earlier lessons, a failure at any tier sends the change back to Development for a real fix, not a workaround applied later in the pipeline.
